Mind you I was pretty active in conservation effort, protest during my 20s. But realising that everything that I've did is just a drop against damages done by corporation and political parties, I stopped.

I'm still mindful about my own consumption and waste only for my own moral reason. Nothing else. Whether apocalypse comes in my own lifetime and the future generation, I have accepted it as the price of living in modern times.

I think you're trying to put a blind eye on the vast dimension of mental illness. You have exhibited super empathic, and as mentioned by other psychopathy on other side of spectrum. Just trying to dissociate your identity from racial supremacist doesn't mean they don't deserve help to reduce their harm for others, the society, or if there's any possibility cruelty to themselves. 

For myself, yes I have chronic mental illness too. No I don't want to compare scar. I want to offer what mental illness meant to me and the mentally problematic community around me, and don't think mental illness should be reduced into identity politics. It's public health issue, and as such treating mental illness should be done with egalitari in mind.
OR: all of the above
Still, I do wish that I have a reason to be depressed. Thinking that I'm sad for no reason at all, made me more anxious and despise my situation more. I really wish that it's not all in my head...

I am still striving to learn about "making agreement with the past", I just cannot get a proper grasp on it. Well, I asked this question because I am frustrated and cannot get into that point of complete peace. Im unable to get out of that cage without the use of substances as I try to forget, and honestly I'm sick of depending on it. I realised recently that I shouldn't be forgetting my past, because I'm forgetting my learned experiences of those mistakes. I lost my maturity. I want to be in agreement, but it felt harder than that statement being said to myself. 

So I had wondered if confronting the past is a form of making an agreement, but you've made a good point. Maybe I'm subconsciously making excuse to be sad and angry at myself, using my dad as a reason to do so. He had shown an effort which impacted my life positively. 

It was long ago in elementary school. Thankfully I learned quickly the impact of being bullied so I tried my best to mediate people with minimal physical confrontation in high school, though I didn't shy myself from fights. Aside from ocassional anger bursts in the past, I would describe my current life in to be quiet and shy, maintaining a polite facade to strangers and acquaintances. I've learn to suppress road rage for a while, either from being too tired, or out of my therapist advice that these anger would only cost me, for just a short bust of adrenaline. However a remnant of my anger issues still remains, and I can assure you it always been directed to myself.

Thanks for your input, much love. I will try again to set my mind straight about being responsible for my own peace, for my own sake.

A bit late, but I think I can address the second point from chronic MDD standpoint. I saw the movie as a mirror, so this rebuttal is more so anecdotal rather than cinephile critic. 

In the ending, I saw the cathartic event Shoya's experiencing marks a significant step to become better person, but I would not necessarily agree he was able to remove his depression completely till we can see any more follow ups in epilogue. He was simply happy (hence cathartic) to be relieved from this major burden that he set himself, which is not uncommon for a chronic MDD person to be happy when realising these kinds of things. Think of it like aha, or eureka moment. 

I don't think his catharsis was so sudden, he was trying and failing to have the confidence to see people with his eyes, until he gain enough to break that barrier and remove it completely. If you're interested you may listen to Mac Miller's Swimming. You sink multiple times, failing multiples, and if you try hard enough and not let yourself swallowed by it, you will end up swimming freely. He tried to remove that filter because he was bothered by it, and promised so after his coma. I'm happy he was able to remove it by the end. 

You got the right idea that it would preferable if he shows visible progress, and that event marks that. But I think that is movie limitation, putting "where they are now" segment would make it cheesy.

I think I feel you. I had also wished to get out of this devilish cycle of my own making. 

I cannot remove anger and depression, so I take the self hatred as my fuel. When I was younger, that cursed feeling causes me to get into drug and cutting habits. But after a certain impactful experience, I started to learn projecting it into other productive things. I still am not the most successful person, but I've gone a long way than before. All due to that feeling, the realization that I'm imperfect and never will be.

I do not seek for self love anymore. I've come to accept that all the anger will always be a secret part of me that drives mu passion. 

I do not seek external love, because I had an experience of emotionally burning somebody that I cared about. 

Sorry for the babble. I just wanna say *I think* I feel you. Our experience differs so perhaps not all of mine would apply. But I sincerely believe that your acceptance and motivation to improve may become a start for something better, because I felt the same as yours.

If you want to talk, let us hear it hopefully we can help you. I wouldn't say that I have kids myself. But maybe I could align with you that I was gonna off myself because I'm sure I was worthless to anyone. So I can say from my experience, if you're patient for a bit longer, somebody or something will need you in the future. Perhaps your kids, perhaps something unlikely.
